sources.entry: How percentile approximation works (and why it's more useful than averages)

summary.title: How Percentiles Work
summary.one_liner: Percentiles describe long-tailed data better than averages, and TimescaleDB percentile approximation hyperfunctions compute them cheaply on large time-series data.
takeaways: Averages are pulled by outliers in long-tailed distributions, while percentiles depend on ordering and are more robust for alerting on user-facing impact.
Exact percentiles in PostgreSQL (percentile_disc, an ordered-set aggregate) must keep all values, which limits memory, parallelism, and continuous aggregate use.
Percentile approximation hyperfunctions use fixed-size, histogram-like partial states that can be parallelized and re-aggregated in continuous aggregates.
The usage pattern is percentile_agg(column) inside a query, with approx_percentile(p, ...) pulling out the desired percentile.
summary.summary: The article explains what averages, medians and percentiles measure, using normal and long-tailed API response time distributions to show why averages can produce false alarms. It then shows exact percentiles in PostgreSQL with percentile_disc and explains why they are expensive for large time-series data. Finally it introduces TimescaleDB's percentile approximation hyperfunctions (percentile_agg with approx_percentile), which use fixed-size partial states that work with parallelism and continuous aggregates. The page is mostly conceptual with a few SQL examples.
